updates.summary: Policy guide setting the architecture of Egypt's National AI Governance Framework, authorised for release in March 2026. Under a 'State as Orchestrator' model, the National Council sets policy and sectoral regulators enforce it. AI systems fall into four tiers: prohibited (e.g. social profiling, exploitation of children, manipulative interference); high-risk (e.g. critical infrastructure, biometrics), needing a 'Dual-Check' of an ethical impact assessment and a technical audit before market entry, then monitoring and serious-incident reporting; limited-risk (chatbots, deepfakes), with disclosure and labelling; and minimal-risk. General-purpose AI with systemic risk counts as high-risk.

Its 'Egypt National AI Regulatory System' initiative plans a Center for Responsible AI, guidelines and standards for classifying AI system risks, detailed guidelines for the Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI, regulations for AI testing and deployment, an AI assurance framework, and an AI law with bylaws and a regulatory body to protect citizens against high-risk or prohibited AI.
updates.notes: The strategy opens with a statement by the President of the Republic launching the second edition, which builds on the first National AI Strategy launched in May 2021. A second governance initiative covers global and regional AI dialogues, including unified Arab AI standards. Most of the strategy concerns economic and capacity goals for 2030 across 21 initiatives, such as an ICT contribution of 7.7% to GDP, 30,000 AI professionals and more than 250 successful AI companies.
updates.scope_note: Mainly an AI adoption and economic development strategy; included for its governance pillar, which commits to an AI regulatory system, an AI law and rules for safe AI testing and deployment.

updates.summary: Eight-article private member's bill setting a regulatory framework for the development and use of AI. It defines AI and AI operators (providers, distributor-users, importers, distributors) and makes safety, transparency, fairness, accountability and privacy mandatory principles. It requires risk assessment, with special measures for high-risk systems, which must be registered with the relevant supervisory authorities and undergo conformity assessment, empowers those authorities to audit compliance, and sets fines of up to TRY 35 million or 7% of annual turnover for prohibited AI practices, TRY 15 million or 3% for breaches of obligations and TRY 7.5 million or 1.5% for false information.
updates.notes: Received by the TBMM Presidency on 24 June 2024 and referred on 25 June 2024 to the Industry, Trade, Energy, Natural Resources, Information and Technology Committee as lead committee and to the Justice Committee as secondary committee, where it remains. The bill would enter into force on publication. It does not define which systems are high-risk, name the supervisory authorities or list the prohibited practices its fines refer to. 'Distributor-user' renders dağıtıcı/kullanıcı, defined as a person who distributes AI systems commercially or uses them in their own activities. A later private member's bill on AI provisions in the Turkish Penal Code and other laws (2/3358) is TR-02.

It sets eight principles: do no harm; ensure robustness, security and safety; avoid perpetuating bias and discrimination; protect the environment; safeguard privacy; promote transparency; develop a human-centred approach; and assign ultimate accountability to humans. It calls for risk evaluations before deployment, robustness testing, continuous monitoring, discrimination impact assessments, bias audits, human intervention and appeal for consequential decisions, and external audits of systems that inform significant decisions.

The guidelines are aligned with UNESCO and OECD standards and refer to the National Cyber Security Agency's 'Guidelines for Secure Adoption and Usage of Artificial Intelligence' for risk evaluation and security standards.

updates.summary: Bilingual Arabic-English code of ethics prepared by the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship under Jordan's 2020 AI Policy and approved by the Council of Ministers, which circulated it to government bodies for compliance. It sets eight principles for the responsible use of AI (humanity and society; inclusiveness and justice; privacy and data; transparency; responsibility and accountability; reliability; integrity and non-fakeness; environment and sustainability), including human intervention in AI decisions, no use of AI to manipulate or mislead, testing before market release and accountability of natural persons for harm. It adds principles for the metaverse and AI research.
updates.notes: The code cites as its legal basis Article 3(d) of the Telecommunications Law No. 13 of 1995, Article 61 of the General Policy for the Communications, Information Technology and Postal Sectors of 2018, and Article 21 of the Jordan Artificial Intelligence Policy 2020, which requires national regulatory frameworks for the responsible use of AI. The Ministry prepared it through a technical committee of experts from the public and private sectors, civil society and academia. It addresses individuals, public and private institutions, international and local organisations and civil society, inside or outside Jordan, and recommends complaint channels at the Ministry for AI-ethics complaints. It also lists the risks of not adhering to it. The Arabic title translates literally as 'National Charter for Artificial Intelligence Ethics'.

updates.summary: Strategy to 2028 with four objectives, six orientations and 52 actions under a vision of ethical, trustworthy AI as a catalyst of the Plan Sénégal Émergent. Orientation 6, 'AI in full confidence', sets out sixteen governance actions: a national consultation, an audit of regional and international ethical and legal recommendations, categorising AI types by their risks to human rights and societal well-being, a balanced and flexible AI regulation, a prefiguration body and then a regulator for emerging technologies, a national ethics committee, regulatory sandboxes and mandatory impact assessments for designated AI types, with soft law in the interim.
updates.notes: The published document is a summary version ('version résumée', 20 pages) dated 2023, produced with technical assistance from Expertise France under the AU-EU D4D Hub project. The minister presented the strategy publicly on 14 September 2023 as a first restitution of the work, open to public contributions, and announced that a final version would be submitted to the head of state for political validation. The OECD.AI entry gives 2024 as its start year and lists it as active. Besides orientation 6, the strategy proposes reaffirming in law the principles that multinational platforms must respect, drawing on the EU's Digital Services Act, Digital Markets Act and AI Act, and plans to train about 90,000 people in data science and AI by 2028.

updates.summary: Five-year strategy approved by the Council of Ministers on 18 January 2023, organised in four programmes and 123 actions. Programme 4 sets up the governance framework for AI and big data so that ethics and liability questions are mastered: Action 4.1 provides for a text on AI ethics and liability within twelve months, to be reflected in the Digital Code and Penal Code and to institute impact analyses and controls of AI solutions over their lifecycle, and Action 4.2 for a controlled environment for AI initiatives under articles 406-408 of the Digital Code pending an AI regulatory body. The controls to be instituted under Action 4.1 are to ensure that AI systems take account of concepts such as transparency, justice and equity, responsibility, non-maleficence, privacy, freedom and autonomy.
updates.scope_note: Mainly a strategy for AI and big-data use cases, skills, research and data management; included as Benin's national AI strategy, whose fourth programme sets up AI governance, an AI ethics and liability text and a controlled environment for AI initiatives.
